In this assignment you will work on the data of the **Meltem wind farm**: 12 turbines, 5 years, one record per turbine per day (`meltem_daily.csv`). Read the data dictionary (`meltem_dictionary.md`) first, then look at the data before you compute anything. The four tasks use what we learned in Lectures 4-7: missing values, sampling, time series components and exploratory analysis.

Tasks 2, 3 and 4 work on the original `meltem`, not on `imputed`: the columns they use (`date`, `turbine`, `fault_next7`, `energy_mwh`, `rotor_rpm`, `gbx_oil_c`) have no gaps, so imputation does not matter there. In Task 1 work on a copy of `meltem` and leave `meltem` itself unchanged.

```{r fixed, cache=F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr); library(ggplot2); library(DMwR2); library(mice)
```

### TASK 1: Missing values (10 points)
`meltem` has missing values. Find all of them and impute them.

Work on a copy of `meltem` and put your result in a data frame named `imputed`, which has the same rows and the same columns as `meltem`. Your imputed values will be compared with the true values (that only the instructor knows): the closer you are, the more points you get. You can lose up to 5 points if you do not explain properly what you did and why.

#### Answer
```{r task1, cache=F}
set.seed(my_seed)
imputed <- meltem                       # work on a copy, meltem stays unchanged
rmse <- function(p, a) sqrt(mean((p - a)^2))

# ---- 1. Find the gaps: explicit NAs and hidden ones (sentinel values) ----
colSums(is.na(imputed))[colSums(is.na(imputed)) > 0]
sapply(imputed %>% select(where(is.numeric)), min)["wind_ms"]   # -9999 is impossible for a wind speed
sum(imputed$wind_ms == -9999)
imputed$wind_ms <- na_if(imputed$wind_ms, -9999)
gap_cols <- c("wind_ms", "gen_temp_c", "vib_gbx_mm_s")

# helper columns (removed at the end): row order and turbine model.
# The two models are visible in the data: one group turns at ~6.8 rpm, the other at ~11 rpm (see Task 4)
imputed <- imputed %>% mutate(.row = row_number()) %>% arrange(turbine, date) %>%
  group_by(turbine) %>% mutate(model = ifelse(mean(rotor_rpm) < 8.5, "big", "small")) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model), turbine = factor(turbine))

# ---- 2. Why are they missing? ----
imputed %>% mutate(month = format(date, "%m")) %>% group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(gap_cols), ~ round(mean(is.na(.x)), 3))) %>% print(n = 12)
# runs of consecutive missing days per column
sapply(gap_cols, function(v) { r <- rle(is.na(imputed[[v]])); round(mean(r$lengths[r$values]), 1) })
imputed %>% group_by(vib_missing = is.na(vib_gbx_mm_s)) %>%
  summarise(gbx_brg_c = mean(gbx_brg_c), rotor_rpm = mean(rotor_rpm), energy = mean(energy_mwh), n = n())
max(imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s, na.rm = TRUE)  # the sensor range ends at 9 mm/s

# ---- 3a. wind_ms: MCAR, single days -> power-curve regression per model + same-day farm residual ----
f_wind <- wind_ms ~ model * (poly(energy_mwh, 3) + gen_rpm + rotor_rpm + pitch_1_deg + pitch_2_deg + pitch_3_deg)
fill_wind <- function(d, use) {           # use = rows whose wind_ms may be used for fitting
  fit <- lm(f_wind, d[use, ])
  res <- ifelse(use, d$wind_ms - predict(fit, d), NA)
  day <- ave(res, d$date, FUN = function(z) if (all(is.na(z))) 0 else mean(z, na.rm = TRUE))
  predict(fit, d) + day
}
# check: hide 1000 known values
obs  <- which(!is.na(imputed$wind_ms)); test <- sample(obs, 1000)
use  <- !is.na(imputed$wind_ms); use[test] <- FALSE
p    <- fill_wind(imputed, use)
c(median = rmse(median(imputed$wind_ms[use]), imputed$wind_ms[test]),
  lm_only = rmse(predict(lm(f_wind, imputed[use, ]), imputed[test, ]), imputed$wind_ms[test]),
  lm_plus_day = rmse(p[test], imputed$wind_ms[test]))
miss <- is.na(imputed$wind_ms)
imputed$wind_ms[miss] <- fill_wind(imputed, !miss)[miss]

# ---- 3b. gen_temp_c: MAR (winter, cold generator), blocks of days -> regression + interpolated residual ----
f_gen <- gen_temp_c ~ turbine + gen_wind_u_c + gen_wind_v_c + gen_wind_w_c + gen_bearing_c + nacelle_c + ambient_c + converter_c
fill_gen <- function(d, use) {
  fit <- lm(f_gen, d[use, ])
  res <- ifelse(use, d$gen_temp_c - predict(fit, d), NA)
  res <- ave(res, d$turbine, FUN = function(z) approx(seq_along(z), z, seq_along(z), rule = 2)$y)
  predict(fit, d) + res
}
# check: hide 150 winter blocks of 7 known days (like the real gaps)
known <- which(!is.na(imputed$gen_temp_c) & format(imputed$date, "%m") %in% c("11", "12", "01", "02", "03"))
test  <- unique(unlist(lapply(sample(known, 150), function(i) i:(i + 6))))
test  <- test[test <= nrow(imputed) & !is.na(imputed$gen_temp_c[test])]
use   <- !is.na(imputed$gen_temp_c); use[test] <- FALSE
knn_d <- imputed %>% select(gen_temp_c, gen_wind_u_c, gen_wind_v_c, gen_wind_w_c, gen_bearing_c, nacelle_c, ambient_c, converter_c) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% mutate(gen_temp_c = ifelse(use, gen_temp_c, NA))
c(mean = rmse(mean(imputed$gen_temp_c[use]), imputed$gen_temp_c[test]),
  mice_norm = rmse(complete(mice(knn_d, m = 1, method = "norm.predict", printFlag = FALSE))$gen_temp_c[test], imputed$gen_temp_c[test]),
  lm_only = rmse(predict(lm(f_gen, imputed[use, ]), imputed[test, ]), imputed$gen_temp_c[test]),
  lm_plus_resid = rmse(fill_gen(imputed, use)[test], imputed$gen_temp_c[test]))
miss <- is.na(imputed$gen_temp_c)
imputed$gen_temp_c[miss] <- fill_gen(imputed, !miss)[miss]

# ---- 3c. vib_gbx_mm_s: censored above 9 mm/s (MNAR) -> Tobit regression, E[y | x, y > 9] ----
X <- model.matrix(~ turbine + model:(wind_ms + gen_rpm + energy_mwh + rotor_rpm) + gbx_oil_c + gbx_brg_c +
                    vib_nac_x_mm_s + vib_nac_y_mm_s + vib_tower_mm_s + ambient_c, imputed)
tobit <- function(X, y, cens, c0) {        # maximum likelihood, base R optim
  nll <- function(par) { b <- par[-length(par)]; s <- exp(par[length(par)]); mu <- drop(X %*% b)
    -sum(ifelse(cens, pnorm((c0 - mu) / s, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE), dnorm(y, mu, s, log = TRUE))) }
  start <- c(lm.fit(X[!cens, ], y[!cens])$coefficients, log(sd(y[!cens])))
  o <- optim(start, nll, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 2000))
  list(b = o$par[-length(o$par)], s = exp(o$par[length(o$par)]))
}
cond_mean <- function(mu, s, c0) { a <- (c0 - mu) / s; mu + s * dnorm(a) / pnorm(a, lower.tail = FALSE) }
# check by simulation: among the known values, pretend the sensor stopped at 8 mm/s
ok <- !is.na(imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s); Xo <- X[ok, ]; yo <- imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s[ok]; c8 <- yo > 8
t8 <- tobit(Xo, ifelse(c8, 0, yo), c8, 8); ols <- lm.fit(Xo[!c8, ], yo[!c8])$coefficients
c(n_hidden = sum(c8), ols = rmse(drop(Xo %*% ols)[c8], yo[c8]),
  ols_floored = rmse(pmax(drop(Xo %*% ols), 8)[c8], yo[c8]),
  tobit = rmse(cond_mean(drop(Xo %*% t8$b), t8$s, 8)[c8], yo[c8]))
# real fit with the true limit 9
cens <- is.na(imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s)
t9 <- tobit(X, ifelse(cens, 0, imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s), cens, 9); mu <- drop(X %*% t9$b)
# does the model explain WHICH rows are missing? predicted vs observed share of gaps
data.frame(mu_bin = cut(mu, c(0, 7.5, 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 12)), p_pred = pnorm((9 - mu) / t9$s, lower.tail = FALSE), gap = cens) %>%
  group_by(mu_bin) %>% summarise(n = n(), predicted = round(mean(p_pred), 3), observed = round(mean(gap), 3))
imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s[cens] <- cond_mean(mu, t9$s, 9)[cens]

# ---- 4. Plots: the vibration histogram is cut at 9; filled values continue it ----
imputed %>% mutate(filled = cens) %>%
  ggplot(aes(vib_gbx_mm_s, fill = filled)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 9, linetype = 2) + labs(title = "vib_gbx_mm_s: observed (cut at 9) and imputed", x = "mm/s") +
  theme_minimal()

# ---- 5. Back to the original order and columns ----
imputed <- imputed %>% arrange(.row) %>% mutate(turbine = as.character(turbine)) %>% select(all_of(names(meltem)))
c(same_dim = identical(dim(imputed), dim(meltem)), any_na = anyNA(imputed),
  same_keys = all(imputed$date == meltem$date & imputed$turbine == meltem$turbine))
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
For every column that has gaps: what is the problem with its gaps, which method did you choose and why, and how did you check that your choice is good?

Three columns have gaps. I checked methods by hiding known values (RMSE).

**`wind_ms`** has no NAs but 1,113 `-9999` values (an impossible speed), which I turned into NAs with `na_if`. They are MCAR: about 5% in every month, single days (mean run 1.1). I used a regression per model on energy, rpm and pitch, plus the same-day mean residual of the other turbines (shared weather). 1,000 hidden values: median 2.07, regression 0.45, regression plus same-day correction **0.22**.

**`gen_temp_c`** (1,381 NAs) is MAR: 22% of January but 0% of June is missing, in blocks of about 8 days, on cold days (winding 42.6 vs 52.7 °C). A mean would be biased. It follows the winding and bearing temperatures (r = 0.95–0.96), so I used a regression on them plus the turbine. Consecutive residuals correlate at 0.83, so I added the residual interpolated in time. Hidden 7-day winter blocks: mean 7.86, mice 1.61, regression 1.30, regression plus residual **0.99**.

**`vib_gbx_mm_s`** (990 NAs) is censored (MNAR). The sensor stops at 9 mm/s, the maximum is exactly 9.00, and the gaps are windy days (40 vs 18 MWh). These values were above 9, but OLS or kNN fill below 9. I fitted a Tobit model (maximum likelihood with `optim`) and used E[y | x, y > 9]. In a simulation hiding the values above 8, the RMSE was 0.80 for OLS and **0.33** for Tobit. It also predicts where gaps fall (93% predicted vs 96% observed when mu > 9.5).


### TASK 2: A fair training/test split (6 points)
We want to build a model that predicts the target `fault_next7` from the other columns. You do **not** build the model. Create a training sample and a test sample from the original `meltem` table for this purpose. Start your code with `set.seed(my_seed)`.

Put your result in a data frame named `split` with the three columns `date`, `turbine` and `set`, one row for every `meltem` row that you use, where `set` is `"train"` or `"test"`. Rows that you do not use are simply not in `split`. Your split will be checked for being fair.

#### Answer
```{r task2, cache=F}
set.seed(my_seed)
d <- meltem %>% arrange(turbine, date)

# rows are not independent: fault_next7 comes in runs (one repair = 7 positive days in a row)
d %>% group_by(turbine) %>% summarise(lag1_autocorr = round(cor(head(fault_next7, -1), tail(fault_next7, -1)), 2)) %>%
  summarise(min = min(lag1_autocorr), max = max(lag1_autocorr))
# and one day is shared by all 12 turbines (same weather): energy of two turbines on the same day
cor(d$energy_mwh[d$turbine == "T01"], d$energy_mwh[d$turbine == "T03"])

# time-ordered split: train on the past (2020-2023), test on the future (2024, a full year = every season once).
# The label of a day looks 7 days ahead, so the last 7 days before the test year are dropped:
# their labels would be decided by events inside the test period.
test_start <- as.Date("2024-01-01"); gap_days <- 7
split <- d %>%
  mutate(set = case_when(date >= test_start ~ "test",
                         date <  test_start - gap_days ~ "train",
                         TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(set)) %>% select(date, turbine, set)

# ---- checks ----
chk <- split %>% left_join(meltem %>% select(date, turbine, fault_next7, energy_mwh), by = c("date", "turbine"))
chk %>% group_by(set) %>% summarise(rows = n(), share = round(n() / nrow(chk), 3), first = min(date), last = max(date),
                                    turbines = n_distinct(turbine), positive_rate = round(mean(fault_next7), 4),
                                    mean_energy = round(mean(energy_mwh), 1))
# number of fault events (runs of 1s) per set
chk %>% arrange(turbine, date) %>% group_by(turbine, set) %>%
  summarise(events = sum(diff(c(0, fault_next7)) == 1), .groups = "drop") %>% group_by(set) %>% summarise(events = sum(events))
# no row twice, no day on both sides, the gap is there, every month of the year in both sets
c(duplicates = sum(duplicated(split[, c("date", "turbine")])),
  shared_days = length(intersect(split$date[split$set == "train"], split$date[split$set == "test"])),
  days_between = as.numeric(min(split$date[split$set == "test"]) - max(split$date[split$set == "train"])))
table(format(split$date, "%m"), split$set)[1:3, ]
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
How did you build the two samples, why is this a fair split for *this* data, and which checks did you do?

The rows are not independent, so a random row split would not be fair. `fault_next7` comes in runs: one repair gives 7 positive days, and the lag-1 autocorrelation of the target is 0.85–0.86 for every turbine. A random split would put days of the same fault event on both sides. In addition, all turbines share the same weather (the daily energy of T01 and T03 correlates at 0.93), so a test day would be explained by other turbines on the same day in training.

So I used a **time-ordered split**: train on the past, test on the future, as the model would be used. The test set is the full year 2024 (4,392 rows, 20.1%), which covers every season and all 12 turbines. The training set runs from 2020-01-01 to 2023-12-24 (17,448 rows). I left out the last 7 days of 2023 (84 rows) because their label looks 7 days into the test year. Each day goes completely to one side.

Checks: no duplicates, no day in both sets, an 8-day gap between the sets, and all 12 turbines and all 12 calendar months in both sets. The positive rate is 2.14% in train and 1.59% in test, with 53 and 10 fault events, so both sets contain positives. The test rate is lower because 2024 had fewer repairs (70 fault days, against 95–115 in 2021–2023). A fair test should report this honestly.


### TASK 3: Time series components (7 points)
Build the series of the **average daily farm energy per month** from the original `meltem` table: for each day add up `energy_mwh` of the 12 turbines, then average these daily totals within every calendar month. You should get 60 values, from January 2020 to December 2024. As a check, the value of January 2020 is 119.9 MWh per day. Make it a monthly time series (`ts`) and decompose it with `stl`.

Draw the decomposition and evaluate it: what do the trend, the seasonal and the remainder components tell about the farm? Use the autocorrelation function (`acf`) to judge the remainder.

#### Answer
```{r task3, cache=F}
monthly <- meltem %>%
  group_by(date) %>% summarise(farm_mwh = sum(energy_mwh), .groups = "drop") %>%     # daily farm total
  mutate(month = format(date, "%Y-%m")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>% summarise(mwh_per_day = mean(farm_mwh), .groups = "drop")      # monthly average
nrow(monthly); round(monthly$mwh_per_day[1], 1)                                       # 60 values, 119.9

energy_ts <- ts(monthly$mwh_per_day, start = c(2020, 1), frequency = 12)
dec <- stl(energy_ts, s.window = "periodic")
plot(dec, main = "STL decomposition of average daily farm energy (MWh/day)")

comp <- dec$time.series
round(comp[1:12, "seasonal"], 1)                                     # the seasonal pattern, Jan..Dec
round(range(comp[, "trend"]), 1); round(aggregate(energy_ts, FUN = mean), 1)   # trend and yearly means
round(c(sd_seasonal = sd(comp[, "seasonal"]), sd_trend = sd(comp[, "trend"]), sd_remainder = sd(comp[, "remainder"])), 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(energy_ts, main = "ACF: raw series", lag.max = 36)
acf(comp[, "remainder"], main = "ACF: remainder", lag.max = 36)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
r_acf <- acf(comp[, "remainder"], plot = FALSE, lag.max = 24)$acf[-1]
round(r_acf[1:3], 2); sum(abs(r_acf) > 2 / sqrt(length(energy_ts)))   # lags outside the 95% band (of 24)
Box.test(comp[, "remainder"], lag = 12, type = "Ljung-Box")
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
Describe the trend, the seasonality and the remainder, and say what the `acf` plot shows and what that means.

The series has 60 values, and January 2020 is 119.9 MWh/day. I used `s.window = "periodic"` because five years are too short to estimate a changing seasonal pattern.

**Seasonality** is the largest component (sd 66.4). It peaks in July (+118) and August (+92) and is lowest in December (−85). The summer–winter difference (about 200 MWh/day) is as large as the mean level. This is the *meltem*, the Aegean summer wind: most of the energy comes in June–September.

**Trend** (sd 25.5) rises from 173 to 255 MWh/day. The yearly means are 186, 214, 249, 244 and 251, so production grows until 2022 and then stays flat. The wind did not cause this: the mean wind changed only from 7.0 to 7.3 m/s, while the energy per m/s rose from 2.22 to 2.87. The farm itself became more productive (for example, higher availability).

**Remainder** (sd 35.1) is larger than the trend. It contains unusual months such as June 2023 (+103) and April 2023 (−74), which are weather anomalies or outages. The ACF of the raw series shows a seasonal wave with a peak at lag 12. This wave is gone from the remainder, but the remainder is not white noise: lags 2–3 are −0.37 and −0.26, 4 of the 24 lags are outside the band, and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.00005. A strong month tends to be followed by weaker ones 2–3 months later. So some structure is left, and a forecast should use lags as well as trend and season.


### TASK 4: Exploratory analysis (7 points)
The farm has two turbine models with different rated power. The file does not say which turbine has which model. Use the whole original `meltem` table.

**4.1** Find out from the data which turbines belong to the larger model. Draw the plots that show it, and write the ids of the turbines of the larger model in your explanation.

**4.2** Compute the correlation between `rotor_rpm` and `gbx_oil_c` (i) over all rows, (ii) over the rows of the turbines of the larger model, (iii) over the rows of the turbines of the smaller model. Draw one scatter plot of `rotor_rpm` against `gbx_oil_c` that shows the finding.

**4.3** Evaluate your findings.

#### Answer
```{r task4, cache=F}
# ---- 4.1 Which turbines are the larger model? ----
per_turbine <- meltem %>% group_by(turbine) %>%
  summarise(mean_energy = mean(energy_mwh), max_energy = max(energy_mwh), q99_energy = quantile(energy_mwh, 0.99),
            mean_rpm = mean(rotor_rpm), max_rpm = max(rotor_rpm), mean_gen_rpm = mean(gen_rpm)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_energy))
per_turbine %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))

ggplot(meltem, aes(reorder(turbine, -energy_mwh, FUN = max), energy_mwh)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Daily energy per turbine: five turbines reach ~69 MWh/day, seven stop near ~45",
       x = "turbine (ordered by maximum)", y = "energy (MWh/day)") + theme_minimal()

big_ids <- per_turbine$turbine[per_turbine$max_energy > 55]
big_ids
m4 <- meltem %>% mutate(model = ifelse(turbine %in% big_ids, "larger model", "smaller model"))

# the two groups also differ in how they reach their power: the larger model turns slower
ggplot(m4, aes(rotor_rpm, energy_mwh, colour = model)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(title = "Energy against rotor speed: two separate power curves", x = "rotor speed (rpm)", y = "energy (MWh/day)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

# ---- 4.2 Correlation between rotor_rpm and gbx_oil_c ----
cors <- c(all_rows = cor(m4$rotor_rpm, m4$gbx_oil_c),
          larger   = with(filter(m4, model == "larger model"),  cor(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c)),
          smaller  = with(filter(m4, model == "smaller model"), cor(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c)))
round(cors, 2)
m4 %>% group_by(turbine, model) %>% summarise(r = round(cor(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c), 2), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(model) %>% summarise(min_r = min(r), max_r = max(r))
m4 %>% group_by(model) %>% summarise(mean_rpm = round(mean(rotor_rpm), 1), mean_oil = round(mean(gbx_oil_c), 1))

ggplot(m4, aes(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = model), alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = model), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Simpson's reversal: r = %.2f over all rows (dashed), but %.2f and %.2f within each model",
                       cors[1], cors[2], cors[3]),
       x = "rotor speed (rpm)", y = "gearbox oil temperature (°C)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ---- 4.3 supporting numbers: oil temperature at the same rpm, and against wind/energy ----
m4 %>% filter(rotor_rpm >= 8, rotor_rpm <= 10) %>% group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_oil_at_8_10_rpm = round(mean(gbx_oil_c), 1))
m4 %>% group_by(model) %>% summarise(r_oil_energy = round(cor(gbx_oil_c, energy_mwh), 2),
                                     r_oil_ambient = round(cor(gbx_oil_c, ambient_c), 2))
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
Which turbines are the larger model, and how did you recognise them? What do the three correlations tell about the relation between rotor speed and gearbox oil temperature? What would you tell the maintenance engineers of the farm?

**4.1** The larger model is **T02, T05, T06, T09 and T11**. Rated power shows up as the ceiling of daily energy. These five turbines reach 64–70 MWh/day (99th percentile 57–60), and the other seven stop at 43–48 (38–40). No turbine falls in between, so the boxplot splits into two groups. The power-curve plot confirms it: the larger model turns much more slowly (mean 6.8 rpm, max about 10) than the smaller one (10.9 rpm, max about 16), as larger rotors do.

**4.2** Over all rows r = **−0.37**. Within the larger model r = **+0.65**, within the smaller model r = **+0.67**, and every single turbine lies between 0.65 and 0.68. This is Simpson's reversal. Within each model, a faster rotor (more wind and load) means hotter oil. But the slow, larger model runs much hotter (66.5 vs 39.4 °C, and 75.8 vs 33.5 °C at the same 8–10 rpm). When the groups are pooled, the slope therefore points the wrong way.

**4.3** The pooled number is misleading. The real relation is positive and the same in both models, but the oil temperature level depends on the model. For the maintenance engineers: set oil temperature alarms **per model**, or better per model and load. With one farm-wide limit, the larger turbines would always be in alarm, and an overheating smaller turbine would never trigger it. Oil temperature also follows ambient temperature (r = 0.93–0.94), so compare it with the value expected for the current load and weather.

```{r final, echo=FALSE}
key3 <- c("date", "turbine", "set")
```
